items.text: I’ll recheck the saved circularity moves with balance weighted more heavily—2×, 3×, 5×, and 10×. I’ll distinguish which recorded moves would be rejected from what would require a new simulation.

items.text:
**Increasing balance’s weight would block some harmful moves, but not most of them.**

I checked the **70 accepted circularity-direction moves after 258**. Of these, **19 increased the reported median badness**.

Replace the current score with:
\[
B_i=(1-C_i)+\lambda\,\frac{\widehat G_i}{59.86}.
\]

Here \(\lambda>1\) gives balance more importance.

| Balance multiplier \(\lambda\) | Recorded moves failing the endpoint test | Of the 19 harmful moves |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 — current | 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 19 | **6** |
| 3 | 24 | **7** |
| 5 | 26 | **7** |
| 10 | 28 | **7** |

**Why does the benefit level off?** In the other **12 harmful moves**, the moving cell’s *modeled gap actually improved*. Giving balance more weight therefore makes their endpoints more attractive. Their harm comes from effects on neighbors or differences between modeled weights and refreshed pickup weights.

There is also a tradeoff: each tested higher multiplier rejects **four moves that reduced the reported median badness**.

One clarification: “circularity move” currently means **the initial direction comes from circularity’s gradient**. Acceptance tests the combined score; it does not require circularity itself to improve throughout the move.

**A 2× or 3× balance weight is a reasonable experiment**, but weighting alone will not solve the neighbor-damage problem.

These are checks of the **same recorded endpoints**, not a rerun. A changed rule could shorten moves, reject them along the path, and change subsequent selections and geometry.

items.text:
**Your concern is supported, especially for circularity moves.** From state 258 to 500, median badness rose from **0.4859 to 0.5275**.

It wasn’t a majority of turns: 61 increased the median, 62 decreased it, and 119 left it unchanged. The increases were larger overall.

| Turn type | Accumulated change in median badness |
|---|---:|
| Circularity moves | **+0.0870** — worse |
| Gap moves | +0.0021 |
| Departure–insertion | **−0.0475** — better |

Three reasons explain this:

1. **Acceptance protects only the moving cell.** It can improve while worsening its neighbors. At selection 260, cell 10’s own badness improved, but the overall median increased.
2. **The frozen-density model is approximate.** All 152 accepted ordinary moves improved the moving cell’s modeled grade, but 69 worsened its grade when weights were subsequently refreshed from pickups. That is a model limitation—not a reason to introduce the count-based acceptance you rejected.
3. **Insertion is unconditional.** Geometric splitting has no grade-improvement guarantee.

**Your proposed “leave reasonably good cells alone” rule is worth testing.** A parameter-free, distributed version would be:

\[
\text{Allow an ordinary move only if }
B_i>\operatorname{median}_{j\in N_i} B_j.
\]

Otherwise the cell sleeps until a neighbor’s change makes it eligible again. Keep departure eligibility separate.

There is supporting evidence: **55 actual changes involved cells already below the global median badness**, and their accumulated contribution was **+0.0650**. That is diagnostic evidence, not proof that suppressing them would improve a rerun.

This local sleeping rule would concentrate effort on worse cells—including cells like 58—but **would not guarantee monotonic improvement**. Preventing neighbor damage would additionally require changing the moving-cell-only acceptance rule.

Yes—at **264 its weight is 130**. I quoted the earlier state at 258.

Its weight can change when **neighboring centers move**, even before center 58 gets its own turn. It remains unselected until **330**, despite its higher weight.

items.text:
You’re right—the labeling is confusing. **Most numbers are cell weights, not cell IDs**, so they change when boundaries move. Only “ID 60” and “ID 49” identify centers.

Between these maps:

- Center **60** leaves its old location and is inserted near center **49**.
- Center **49** also moves as part of the geometric split.
- Surrounding centers keep their IDs and positions, but their boundaries—and therefore weights—can change.

So the changing numbers do not establish that cell identities were mixed up. But this figure makes tracking identities difficult.

The clear format is **a permanent ID at each center, with weight shown only by color**. I should have used that.
